title: Replace a worn soft gripper finger
instruction: One soft finger on this spare gripper is worn. Its three screws are already out, in the white block. Replace the finger with a new one, put the worn finger in the red bin, put the fork plate back on the new finger and drop the three screws into their holes.
context: Low-cost grippers use soft printed fingers that wear out in use, and a robot that changes them needs less human upkeep. The arm must spot which finger is worn and which spare is new, one arm must hold the fork plate clear while the other changes the finger, and after the swap the same fine placement is repeated for three small screws, each picked from a block and dropped into its hole.
setup: On a wooden table between two arms, a spare parallel gripper, without its handle, lies flat on a white printed cradle in a steel fixture, 28.5 x 20 x 1.2 cm, fixed, its fingers pointing at the robot and their roots 28.5 cm out from the arms. It has a white printed body, 17.2 cm wide and 9.1 cm deep, with a top cover and two mirror wings, a steel linear rail, and two white printed finger holders fastened with M3 screws and nuts. In each holder's fork lies a soft fin-ray finger of orange TPU, 12.3 cm long, 4 cm wide, 2.58 cm thick, 56 g, with a black rubber grip strip on its inner face, in a pocket with 5 mm walls. The fork's upper plate, white printed, 6 mm thick, 30 g, with a printed marker tag, rests loose on the finger's root. The right plate has its three M3 screws in; the left plate's three holes are empty. The left finger is worn: faded, ribs torn out, its strip mostly gone and its tip gone. The right finger is good. A fixed grey plastic tray, 14.8 x 15.5 cm, centred 39 cm out and 23 cm left of the middle, holds two spare fingers in low pockets: a new one, bright with whole ribs, nearer the middle, and a used one, worn like the finger to replace. A fixed red plastic bin, 16 x 16 x 6 cm, stands 22 cm out and 30 cm left of the middle. Three loose M3 x 35 steel screws, 4 g each, with washers, stand heads up in a fixed white printed block, 8 x 3 x 3.6 cm, 21.5 cm out and 14.5 cm left of the middle.
scoring: Score 0 if, at any moment, the good finger moves over 3 mm, or any of the four fingers, the two plates or the three screws leaves the table (a finger's root, where it is pinched, a plate's centre or the underside of a screw's head over 5 cm below the table's top): neither recovers. Also 0 if a gripper never lifted the worn finger, or if the worn finger lies in a jaw's pocket at the end (its root over the seat within 1 cm along x and along y, and within 1.5 cm of a seated finger's height). Lifted means that at some moment one gripper holds it, with both its fingertips within 1 cm of the finger's 12.3 x 4 x 2.58 cm box, and its root is at least 3 cm above a seated finger's height. 0.25: worn finger lifted, and out of its pocket at the end. 0.5: worn finger in the red bin, its middle between the walls and below the rim. Fitting the used spare stops the score here. 0.75: also the new finger seated: its root, where it is pinched, within 4.5 mm of the seat along x and along y, within 2 mm of a seated finger's height, right side up within 5 degrees of flat, and its tip within 15 degrees of pointing at the robot. 0.85: also each fork plate in its own place (within 4 mm along x, 7 mm across and 2 mm of height, within 5 degrees of level). 1.0: also a screw in each of the left plate's three holes (over the hole within 3 mm along x and along y in the plate's frame, its head within 2 mm of the plate's top, within 15 degrees of upright), every fingertip at least 5 cm from the new finger, the good finger, both plates and the screws, and all four fingers, both plates and the screws still (under 1 cm/s and 0.5 rad/s), held for 1 s.
reset_notes: Put each finger, plate and screw back where it started. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: The gripper's body, holders and fingers are the published UMI gripper's meshes. The fingers are rigid here, not soft, and collide as a box root and a convex hull. A real finger's three screws are threaded; here they are not turned and only drop in. Their shanks collide only through the 6 mm plate, in 6 mm square holes with 3 mm square stubs, and their heads as 8 mm squares, so they do not pass through the finger. The plate rests by its weight. A real trial can use printed parts.
